question: Check mlqrt/Melqart's king-of-the-city analysis and the limits of a fixed merchant-patron/theological profile against an inscription, philological source or scholarly passage.

entry_locators_rechecked.text: The name *mlqrt*, conventionally Melqart, is understood as “king of the city”; its civic semantics are more productive than assigning the god the modern job “patron of merchants” alone (Bonnet 1988).

The Arados base AO 7676, cataloged to 25–24 BCE, pairs Greek Heracles with Phoenician Melqart in a bilingual dedication involving the gymnasium's gods. Its very late date matters: do not project that institutional setting into Bronze Age Tyre.

passages.passage_support: The CIS editor states that the word šmʿ ('he heard') 'very often closes Phoenician inscriptions'. This supports reading the formula as a genre convention: evidence that the dedications share a votive grammar, not a fixed theology of one god. It tempers (does not contradict) round 8's use of the KAI 201 formula.

passages.source_excerpt: The Cippi, two marble pillars from the 2nd century BC, hold immense historical significance due to the bilingual Phoenician and Greek inscriptions they bear. These inscriptions were pivotal in the decipherment of the Phoenician script by French scholar Jean-Jacques Barthélemy in 1758. In 1782, one of the Cippi was gifted to France by Grand Master de Rohan… Since then, it has resided at the Louvre Museum in Paris, while its twin remained in Valletta.

name_analysis_king_of_the_city: No museum or corpus witness retrieved this round states the etymology; the analysis remains passage-supported by round 8's WiBiLex (§1) and Euphrosyne 45 statements.

What this shard adds is epigraphic: the divine name appears consonantal in both primary routes — lmlqrt in the KAI 201 transliteration (retrieval 6) and lmlqrt/wlmlqrt in the Arados Phoenician line as quoted by Aliquot 2025 (retrieval 5). A consonantal script cannot supply the vowels of 'Melqart', so the entry's hedge 'conventionally Melqart' ('understood as') is motivated at object level.
Bonnet's own dedicated name study exists — HAL record hal-01870534, 'Le nom de Melqart' (1992) — but the deposit is metadata-only; recorded as a lead, not a passage.
civic_semantics_object_level: Kition c. 380–370 BCE: Melqart as 'his lord' in a dedication dated by the city-king's regnal year, by a royal interpreter (AO 4826 / CIS I 88).
Malta 2nd c. BCE: 'Melqart, Lord of Tyre' against a Greek archegete (the museum pair, both institutions now named).
Arados 25/24 BCE: Melqart in the translated slot of Herakles in a civic athletic institution's dedication, dated by the civic era (AO 7676, with a 2025 autopsy).

Kition comparators: the same city's dedications to Reshef-Mikal and the compound Esmun-Melqart use the same formula and regnal dating, so Melqart's civic embedding is one instance of a city-pantheon grammar rather than a unique theology.
anti_fixing_merchant_patron: The four object records read this round name these roles only: 'his lord' (lmrʔh), city-king regnal dating, royal interpreter, gods of the gymnasium/palaestra, translated Herakles. None states a merchant-patron job.

The trader-protector wording appears in this lane's evidence base only as the Aubet relay inside the tertiary Wikipedia page (round 8) — one role among many, in a relay, and never as the god's fixed profile.
This is calibrated absence over the retrieved set, not a proof about the literature; a commercial function is not denied by anything retrieved.
translation_relation_greek_phoenician: Aliquot 2025 (retrieval 5) states the two Greek god-names are 'soit transcrit (ʾrms), soit traduit en phénicien (mlqrt)' — transcription for Hermes, translation for Herakles.
